title: Statistical Fluctuations as Primordial Correlators in the CMB: Finite Chemical Potential Thermodynamics
authors: Anish Ghoshal, Anupam Mazumdar, Bartłomiej Sikorski
abstract: Can primordial cosmological correlations originate from statistical fluctuations of an early-universe thermal system? We connect grand-canonical thermodynamics, stochastic transport, and gauge-invariant cosmological perturbations for a charged fluid at finite chemical potential. Energy-charge susceptibilities determine curvature, charge-isocurvature, and cross-correlation amplitudes, while transport sets when each mode leaves equilibrium. For an isolated, adiabatic conformal plasma with conserved charge-to-entropy ratio and power-law diffusion, diffusive freeze-out yields the universal spectrum $\mathcal P_S(k)\propto k^3$, with $n_{\rm iso}=4$, while equal-time local-equilibrium curvature-isocurvature covariance vanishes in the conformal source basis. Thus neither finite chemical potential nor replacing Hubble crossing by diffusion crossing alone yields approximate scale invariance. We evade this obstruction with an open subsystem of massless Dirac fermions during a sourced quasi-de Sitter phase. There, grand-canonical energy cumulants generate a nearly scale-invariant red curvature spectrum. A benchmark gives $\mathcal P_{ζ_X}(k_\star)=2.10\times10^{-9}$ and $n_s(k_\star)=0.9649$, stays within $0.30%$ of the fitted power law over $0.002\leq k/k_\star\leq4$, and predicts weak negative running and small positive intrinsic non-Gaussianity from higher-order cumulants, $f_{\rm NL}(k_\star)\simeq0.106$ and $g_{\rm NL}(k_\star)\simeq0.0158$. With a two-helicity vacuum tensor spectrum, the tensor-to-scalar ratio is $r_{t/s}(k_\star)=1.82\times10^{-4}$. This isolates the limitation of isolated conformal thermal seeding and the open-system ingredient needed to overcome it. Thermal energy-charge fluctuations thus provide a calculable source of realistic scalar correlations, while reservoir dynamics, equilibration, and later curvature-isocurvature transfer must come from a microscopic model.
summary: This paper explores generating primordial cosmological correlations from early-universe thermal fluctuations using a charged fluid model. It establishes that simple, isolated thermal models fail to produce the observed scale-invariant spectra. The authors overcome this by modeling the system as an open subsystem, successfully predicting realistic values for CMB observables like the spectral index and non-Gaussianity.
main_problem: Investigating whether primordial cosmological correlations can arise from the statistical fluctuations of an early-universe thermal system.
main_result: The analysis shows that an isolated conformal plasma cannot generate scale-invariant spectra, but an open system involving massless Dirac fermions can generate a nearly scale-invariant red curvature spectrum matching observational benchmarks.
method: The work connects grand-canonical thermodynamics, stochastic transport theory, and gauge-invariant cosmological perturbation theory.
model_or_system: The system is a charged fluid at finite chemical potential undergoing cosmological evolution, analyzed using the grand-canonical partition function and susceptibility matrix.
key_observables: Primordial power spectra ($\mathcal P_S(k)$), spectral indices ($n_s$), non-Gaussianity parameters ($f_{NL}, g_{NL}$), and the tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r/s$).
important_parameters: Finite chemical potential ($\mu$), conserved charge-to-entropy ratio, and the nature of the system (isolated vs. open subsystem).
main_assumptions: The initial analysis assumes local equilibrium for deriving the covariance matrix; the solution requires considering an open subsystem exchanging energy/charge with a reservoir.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops a framework connecting thermodynamics and cosmology, first analyzing the limitations of isolated systems, and then proposing and calculating results for an open subsystem to achieve scale-invariant predictions.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (stochastic transport) to cosmology provides a deep theoretical link between microscopic thermal fluctuations and macroscopic cosmological observables, relevant for understanding system boundaries and reservoir effects.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Curvature spectrum for the representative solution µ/T⋆= 2 and ΩX = 0.003. The upper panel compares PζX(k)/As (solid blue curve) with the pivot power law (k/k⋆)ns⋆−1 (black dashed curve), using As = 2.10 × 10−9 and ns⋆= 0.9649. The lower panel shows the fractional departure 100[PζX/(As(k/k⋆)ns⋆−1)−1] over 10−3 ≤k/k⋆≤103. Within the fitted interval 0.002 ≤k/k⋆≤4, the maximum absolute residual is 3.003 × 10−3, or approximately 0.30%, demonstrating that the thermal spectrum is accurately described by a weakly running red power law across the range used in the numerical fit.

Figure 2: Scale dependence of the local scalar index ns(k) = 1 + d ln PζX/d ln k for µ/T⋆= 2 and ΩX = 0.003. The solid blue curve is the model prediction and the black dashed line marks the pivot value ns⋆= 0.9649. The index changes only at the level of a few parts in 10−4 over the displayed fitted interval, consistently with the small running αs(k⋆) = −1.66951 × 10−4.

Figure 3: Scale dependence of the local-type cumulant amplitudes for µ/T⋆= 2 and ΩX = 0.003. The upper panel shows fNL(k) and the lower panel shows gNL(k), evaluated using the grand- canonical energy cumulants and the horizon-scale matching prescription. At the pivot, fNL = 0.1055 and gNL = 0.01583. Both quantities vary by less than approximately 10−3 fractionally over the fitted interval.
